---
title: "Set a plot in a sentence"
subtitle: "A sparkline among the words, at the height of the text."
description: "The nanoplot renderers are ordinary Typst functions, so they run inline in prose and follow the surrounding text size."
---

The renderers are not tied to a table.
Each is an ordinary function returning content, so one sits in a line of prose as readily as in a cell.

```typst
#import "@preview/keisen:0.1.0": nanoplot-bar, nanoplot-line, nanoplot-points

#let series = (3.0, 3.4, 3.1, 4.2, 4.0, 4.9)

Revenue rose through the year #nanoplot-line(series, width: 4em), reading
#nanoplot-points(series, width: 4em) by quarter and
#nanoplot-bar(series, width: 4em) by volume, all at #raw("0.8em").

#set text(size: 16pt)
At a larger text size the plots follow it: #nanoplot-line(series, width: 4em).
```

![A line of prose with a sparkline, a marked sparkline, and a bar plot set inline among the words at the height of the text, and below it the same sparkline at a larger text size, drawn correspondingly larger.](../assets/examples/nanoplots-inline.png)

The second line is the point: the plots carry no size of their own, so `set text(size: ..)` moves them with everything else.

Every coordinate is a fraction of the box, so an `em` size needs no absolute resolution and no minimum canvas, which is what lets a nanoplot be the size a nanoplot is meant to be.
`stroke: auto` and `fill: auto` follow the surrounding text colour, so a plot inside a styled run is drawn in that run's ink.

The renderers are drawn with native Typst primitives and come out of the package like everything else, so nothing else is fetched to draw them.
